AW-STUDY-0035 · Oracle study

How the great games design their spaceships

You named three masters: RSI (Star Citizen), Starfield and EVE Online. This study reads how their studios actually build ships, goes through the 27 space games in the Oracle, and turns it into rules for Abbie's World. And the Aurora Mk II you asked about is RSI's: the ground-up redesign of Star Citizen's first starter ship, flyable since this March.

A ship, built the way studios build them

This is a white-box ship, the same stage Star Citizen's pipeline uses: named parts with real pivots, before any final art. It's our own blockout, not any game's model. Try the buttons. They are the mechatronics pass in miniature.

HullMoving partModule (snaps on, adds mass)Light that shows stateFigures: a 1.2 m child and a 1.9 m adult

The short version

  1. A ship is a character before it is a vehicle. Start with who flies it and what it has been through.
  2. One silhouette, read from the back and from far away. Three big volumes, a few medium, many small, and the detail gathered at one focal point.
  3. Shape language is a promise. Round means friendly, a flat belly means it can land, swept means fast, an exposed frame means rugged. Keep a family consistent and families distinct.
  4. Function first: every part says what it's for. Place the cockpit, engines, landing gear, door and ramp before the hull wraps them. This is NASA-punk.
  5. Ships are built from parts, and the parts are the game. Modules snap on, change the silhouette and add mass.
  6. Inside and outside are one ship. Size doors, ladders and seats to the bodies that use them.
  7. Boarding is a ritual: the ramp drops, light spills out, the canopy lifts, the gear unfolds.
  8. Information lives on the ship. Use cockpit screens, glowing engines, warm windows and running lights.
  9. Flight feel comes from thrusters you can see: VTOL fans that swivel and wings that fold.
  10. Damage and upgrades show on the parts.

The three masters

RSI · Star Citizen

A ship is a hierarchy of named parts

Concept artists deliver "upward of 16 different roughs", then a rough 3D model. Engineers check the landing gear, thrusters, cockpit, bunks and weapons before any final art. In the white box the ship is sliced into pieces that can be damaged on their own and are "attached together by code at runtime". Damage, effects, animation and variants all hang off those pieces.

A door built too small for the pilot (the "Hobbins Hole") is why sizes are checked at the concept stage. The Aurora Mk I came in five variants; a cockpit fix used to be made five times, and now it's made once.

RSI · Aurora Mk II

How to make a Mk 2

"Takes the essence of the Mk I and brings it up to a level suitable for the game as it exists today." It keeps three nods to the Mk I: the round side door, the bed and the window. Everything else is new. Four swept wings fold back to land, and the lower wings carry VTOL fans. It's bigger inside so you can walk around and reach the components. It's also the first ship with snap-on external modules (cargo and combat), and they add mass.

24.5 m long and 63.5 t, against the Mk I's 19 m and 27 t. RSI chose modules over variants: one base ship that does "a little bit of most missions".

Bethesda · Starfield

NASA-punk and a kit of parts

"You can draw a line from current-day space technology and extrapolate from there." On the ships that shows up as stencils, hazard stripes, exposed truss and chunky struts. The ship builder snaps cockpits, habs, engines and gear together, and the habs generate the interior. Every hab must connect. The manufacturer (Taiyo, Deimos, Hopetech, Stroud-Eklund, Nova Galactic) changes only the look, never what a part does.

CCP · EVE Online

Shape language per family

Amarr ships are golden cathedrals, Caldari are hard slabs taken from fighter jets and carriers, Gallente have "art nouveau curves", and Minmatar are proud "scrap heaps". The rule is "visual distinction from the other races, and a visual cohesion within each race". In the Rupture redesign, "messy 3D blockouts" found the problems that 2D hides, and warm orange windows say a crowd lives inside. Tech 3 cruisers have five subsystems that change the ship's actual shape, for thousands of combinations.

The other 15 space games in the Oracle (Breathedge, IXION, Dyson Sphere Program, Deliver Us The Moon, The Invincible, Surviving Mars, Sins of a Solar Empire, Ring Runner, Transcendence, VoidExpanse, Entropy, Breachway, ΔV, Empyrion, Space Pirates and Zombies) add little about ship design. Most use fixed hulls where fitted slots change the stats, not the look. All 16 hand-studied games now carry a "How it's drawn" note in the Oracle.

What a ship is made of

Silhouette

Design the rear view first, because that's what the player sees. Check every angle: a sleek ship can "come back looking like a duck". Use two or three tones: ground colours underneath, sky colours on top.

Function

Place the cockpit, engines, gear, door, ramp, sensors and cargo first. Name each part by its job. A part is what gets damaged, animated, upgraded and varied.

Interior

A window promises a room. Doors, ladders, bunks and seats fit both a 1.9 m adult and Abbie's 1.1 m eye height. Leave room to walk to the machinery.

Mechanics

Gear, ramps, canopies, folding wings and swivelling engines. Each one gets a pivot, a range and a sound. Landing and take-off are shots worth watching.

Displays

Diegetic first: cockpit screens, engine glow, warm windows, beacons, red and green running lights. Overlay is only for precise numbers.

Damage and upgrades

Scorch, dent and spark per part; parts can fall off. An upgrade is a new part you can see and feel.

What Abbie's World adopts

  1. Every ship gets a one-line story before anyone draws it.
  2. Silhouette first: from the back, at card size and at 50 m.
  3. A shape language per maker. Some ideas: Aurora Works (round explorers in ivory and sunset orange), Bolt & Bucket (haulers with exposed frames, yellow and rust) and Swiftwing (white and blue racers).
  4. Function first, with kid-readable NASA-punk details: stencils, hatches, hazard stripes.
  5. Named parts with snap points. Modules change both the silhouette and the mass.
  6. The inside matches the outside, at Abbie's size, with a cutaway view that works as the ship's map.
  7. Boarding and landing are the best moments, and the mechatronics pass is where they get made.
  8. State shows on the ship, never on the screen.
  9. Damage and upgrades show on the parts.

Made with Midjourney v8.2 (Relax mode). The prompts and job ids are in docs/oracle/spaceships/concepts/provenance.json. These are our own concepts: they borrow what the study learned and copy no game ship.

Meshy ships

Meshy built all eight ship pictures into 3D, and a Blender pass mirrored each one so it is exactly symmetric. Spin them beside their pictures.

Next: Mk 2 from concept to moving model

  1. You pick the concept art (any of the four in each row).
  2. Meshy turns the pick into a model (done for all eight, untextured, mirrored symmetric).
  3. Blender cleanup, the Bruiser way: low poly, split into named parts at the module seams, real materials.
  4. The mechatronics pass: the gear unfolds in three steps, the VTOL nacelles swivel, the canopy hinges, the ramp drops and the modules snap on. Each part gets a sound.

The brief: a family explorer, our own design. It keeps three signatures of our first ship: a round door, a bunk and a big window. A rear bay takes modules that change the shape and the weight. The nacelles swivel and the gear folds for the landing ritual. The inside is walk-through at Abbie's size, and everything the ship is doing shows on the ship.
